sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Single Leg Kettlebell Stiff Leg Deadlift is a unilateral hip-hinge exercise that isolates the hamstrings and glutes one leg at a time.

Performed standing on one leg while hinging forward with a kettlebell in one hand, this movement demands exceptional balance, coordination, and posterior chain strength.

This exercise is highly effective for correcting muscle imbalances, improving single-leg stability, and building functional hamstring and glute strength that carries over to running, jumping, and sport.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Isolates each leg individually to address strength imbalances
- Deep hamstring and glute stretch under load
- Develops balance, proprioception, and coordination
- Strengthens the stabiliser muscles of the ankle, knee, and hip
- Builds functional single-leg strength for athletic performance
- Improves hip hinge mechanics and posterior chain control
- Low equipment requirement — only a single kettlebell needed

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Hamstrings

Secondary: Glutes, Erector Spinae, Core (Obliques, Rectus Abdominis), Hip Stabilisers, Calves, Forearms and Grip

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Stand with your feet hip-width apart.
2. Hold a kettlebell in one hand with an overhand grip, arm fully extended.
3. Shift your weight onto the opposite leg (if kettlebell is in your right hand, stand on your left leg).
4. Keep a slight bend in the standing knee.
5. Engage your core and pull your shoulders back.
6. Lift your free leg slightly off the ground behind you to prepare.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Stand with your feet hip-width apart, holding a kettlebell in one hand with an overhand grip.
2. Lift one leg off the ground behind you and hinge forward at the hips, keeping your back straight and the kettlebell close to your body.
3. Lower the kettlebell toward the ground while keeping your lifted leg straight and your balance centred over your standing foot.
4. Return to the starting position by contracting your hamstring and glute muscles, and repeat the movement for the desired number of reps before switching to the other leg.
5. Your body and rear leg should form a straight line as you hinge forward.
6. Control the movement throughout — avoid rushing or using momentum.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Rounding the lower back instead of maintaining a flat spine
- Opening the hips by rotating the lifted leg outward
- Bending the standing knee too much, turning it into a squat
- Not hinging deep enough to feel the hamstring stretch
- Letting the kettlebell swing away from the body
- Losing balance by rushing through reps
- Not keeping the hips square and level throughout the movement

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Kettlebell (appropriate weight for single-leg balance)
- Flat, non-slip surface to stand on
- Optional: Exercise mat for foot traction
- Optional: Wall or rack nearby for balance assistance when learning
- Recommended: Start lighter than bilateral RDL — balance is the limiting factor

sections.heading: Choosing Your Kettlebell Weight
sections.content:
1. Beginners: Start with 4-8 kg (men) or 4-6 kg (women).
2. Intermediate: 12-20 kg (men) or 8-12 kg (women).
3. The weight should challenge the hamstrings without compromising balance.
4. If you cannot maintain a level hip position, the weight is too heavy.
5. Master the movement pattern with a light weight before progressing.
6. Balance and control are more important than load in this exercise.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Standing Foot: Firmly planted, weight through the heel and mid-foot.
2. Standing Knee: Slight bend, maintained throughout the hinge.
3. Hips: Square and level — do not let the hip of the raised leg rotate open.
4. Spine: Neutral from head to tailbone.
5. Rear Leg: Extends straight behind you as a counterbalance.
6. Arm: Fully extended, kettlebell hanging straight down.
7. Head: Neutral, eyes looking a few feet ahead on the floor.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Kettlebell RDL (Bilateral): Both feet on the ground, same hip hinge pattern
- Barbell Romanian Deadlift: Heavier loading with both legs
- Single Leg Dumbbell RDL: Same movement using a dumbbell instead
- Single Leg Cable RDL: Cable machine for constant tension
- Good Morning: Barbell on back, bilateral hip hinge
- Nordic Hamstring Curl: Bodyweight hamstring exercise from kneeling

sections.heading: Single Leg Deadlift Variations
sections.content:
Single Leg Kettlebell Stiff Leg Deadlift: Standard single-leg hinge with kettlebell
Contralateral Single Leg RDL: Kettlebell in opposite hand to standing leg
Ipsilateral Single Leg RDL: Kettlebell in same hand as standing leg
Bodyweight Single Leg RDL: No weight, focusing on balance and form
Banded Single Leg RDL: Resistance band for accommodating resistance
Slow Tempo Single Leg RDL: 3-4 second eccentric for time under tension

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Balance Difficulty: Use a wall or rack for light fingertip support
Hamstring Tightness: Reduce hinge depth and increase over time
Lower Back Sensitivity: Focus on core bracing and use a lighter weight
Ankle Instability: Perform barefoot or in flat shoes for better ground contact
Knee Issues: Maintain a consistent soft bend in the standing leg
Learning Stage: Master the bilateral kettlebell RDL before progressing to single leg
